To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Japanese listeners can be trained to identify English /l/ and /r/ in words produced by a single talker in five different phonetic contexts.

training with multiple talkers leads to improved performance, but performance does not transfer to novel tokens from a new talker; training with a single talker leads to improved performance and transfer of learning, but only to a limited extent; and the phonetic environment of the new contrast appears to be an important determinant of learning.

training Japanese listeners to distinguish English /r/ from /l/ results in improved performance and generalization to novel words produced by familiar and unfamiliar talkers, provided that the training tokens are produced by multiple talkers and contain the /r/-l/ contrast in a variety of phonetic contexts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of perceptual learning in the context of speech perception, and the role of variability and talker-specific information in the development of new phonetic categories.
how listeners develop phonetic categories for new phonetic contrasts in a second language.
the role of talker variability and phonetic environment in perceptual learning of non-native contrasts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

perceptual learning of new phonetic categories is a complex and multifaceted phenomenon that is influenced by the nature of the new phonetic contrast, the phonetic environment of the contrast, talker variability, and the listener's native language.
perceptual learning and the formation of phonetic categories are complex, highly variable, and context-dependent processes.
the more variability the better.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more variability there is in the training materials, the more generalizable is the learning.

perceptual learning is a process of selective attention to contrastive dimensions in the speech signal and that this process is influenced by a number of factors that mediate the degree to which a listener can generalize a newly acquired category to novel stimuli.

the acquisition of new perceptual categories is a gradual, dynamic process that is influenced by a variety of factors including the phonetic environment, talker variability, and phonetic similarity to the native language.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perceptual system has the capacity to learn new perceptual categories, but that this capacity is limited by the amount of variability in the training environment.

perceptual learning can be very rapid and robust when the training materials are designed to take into account variability and the perceptual and linguistic factors that influence the learning process.
variability is an important component of category acquisition, and that variability is not just noise.
